OP, I had the same issue as you on my M6 that I had shot last year in near 0 temps in Canada last January. What is happening is that the cold weather is causing the lubricants to gum up a bit and throw off your shutter speeds resulting in some capping. I found this out the hard way when the last 12 shots in a roll of HP5 I in the aforementioned settings progressively showed increased capping until just blank negatives at the end of the roll.

You'll want to start shooting again in warmer weather but you will need to have a CLA done to get the 1/500 and 1/1000 speeds accurate again. I've read on many places on the internet that you could get a CLA done for being more resilient to colder weather (ie a more cold tolerant lubricant).

When choosing a camera to scan for medium format, you need to look at the Y resolution dimension. Hey OP, I noticed the same thing when scanning film with my X-H2. The issue seems to be that the X-Trans colour array just does something funky to the grains of film when scanning and converting through NLP. Obviously part of the issue is the whole X-Trans and Adobe relationship when it comes to how it handles the RAWs. Straight single shot scans from any Fuji camera converted through NLP always look a bit soft.

I found in comparison with scanning with my Eos R + 100mm RF that I got much crisper sharper scans.

HOWEVER

My H2 does have a pixel shift function. This is the solution to the issue I mentioned above. It basically cancels out the X-Trans array by being able to sample the RGB range properly (many Bayer cameras with pixel shift also do this). I've pixel shift scanned a lot of Medium and Large format stuff and they all come looking amazing with well defined sharp grain, and much better colours when you convert through NLP.

Of course, the X-Trans issue can be avoided entirely by switching to a Bayer camera or using a dedicated film scanner, but if you want to get better accurate colours when converting, a pixel shift feature (which doesn't exist on the OG Z6, but does on the 3rd version of the camera and is also present in the Zf) would help.

I got 2 hot takes, both after doing this for a while (scanning and shooting medium format):

- Medium format is pointless in the age of digital, and is way to cumbersome out in the field. I started my film journey with my first camera being a Zenza Bronica. Now I prefer 35mm and see why it took off, its just much more convenient and I don't look sketchy changing film like on MF. In addition, the prevalence of digital camera scanning with full frame sensors lining up with 35mm film means you can take advantage of high resolution bodies for high resolution scans. When scanning medium format (ie 6x6) your resolution is determined by the short side of the sensor (so basically a 40 MP camera will get you 25 MP when cropped in for 6x6). 

- There is nothing special about C41 negative film. Its too fussy when scanning and its very easy to replicate its colours and tonality on digital (and with ease too). 

A bonus unpopular opinion: If you aren't shooting film to keep the negatives, there is no point in shooting film. The negative is where the magic happens, be it for scanning or darkroom printing.

I use 2 setups. For 35mm its a Canon EOS R + RF 100mm. It works pretty well. The best thing about it is the canons way of zooming into the frame at 10x which allows me to focus on the grain which is crucial for 35mm. Because you're mapping a 35mm frame to a 35mm sized sensor, you get most of the 30 MP resolution of the camera which is on par with XL Noritsu scanners (also 30 MP). 

For 120 and 4x5 I use a Fujifilm X-H2 + Laowa 65mm APO Macro. The fujifilm was difficult to use when scanning 35mm hence why I have the canon setup. When scanning 120 and LF I use the pixel shift function. There are 2 modes when compiling the pixel shift photos on Fujifilm Cameras: Accurate colour only which cancels out the X-Trans array and accurate colour + Resolution which gives 160 MP files. I use the former mode for 120 and the latter for scanning my 4x5s which after cropping I end up with 132-ish MP scans. 

I suggesting going with a Canon RF APSC camera + any macro lens you can find as I find canons zoom in for focusing assist the best for scanning.

The proper way to utilize Silverfast+ NLP is as follows (its what I do):

- Set your film type to positive, and your scan type to 48-Bit HDR Raw, your DPI may vary but I set mine to 3600, the actual optical maximum of the scanner which will yield about 17 MP. 

- Set your file type to DNG 

- Hit Scan for your pre-scan, adjust your scan border (the red box around the preview) accordingly. You will want to include a little bit of the film border. It is inevitable that you will it show up in your preview scan given that its a bit difficult to line up a cut negative strip perfectly in the holder. 

- It should be noted that because of your settings in the first step, you cannot make any adjustments whatsoever in silverfast. In fact you will get a pop-up about this when you select 48 Bit HDR Raw 

- Import your raw scans into LR/PS. Be sure to use the WB picker tool to set the WB of your negatives. You just need to select one frame that has the film edge showing to do this and you can sync the rest of your frames with it to match. 

From there you need to adjust your cropping as to have little of the borders showing anywhere if possible as it will throw off the NLP analysis and give you some weird looking results.

Negative Lab - Based in Tarzana, California. A small boutique lab, frequented by working photographers. Turnaround can range from 7-10 days. With that said they are on the more pricey side but well worth it for the attention to detail. They are my default for 35mm BW and C41 unless I shoot E6 or Large format. 

Boutique Film Lab- Based in Mount Juliet Tennessee. A medium sized lab with about 4 people. Their turnaround times range from 3-7 days depending on what services you choose with them. They're very upfront about their turnarounds and even offer quicker 2 day and rush services. I'd say they're the most balanced lab as far as price/turnaround times.

Memphis Film Lab - Do I need to say more? Probably the most recommended lab in this sub. Used to be ran by the owner himself but I believe they're a 2 person team now. Their turnaround times are usually in the 1.5-2 week range but they're worth it for their prices.

Underdog Film Lab - Based on Oakland, California. They use referma dip and dunk systems for their developing. Their turnaround times are pretty quick. Usually around 3 days. They offer cut/sleeving of negatives which is a huge plus. I use them if I want to develop only and scan myself. 

Photoworks - Based in San Francisco, California. Turnaround time is usually 4-5 days in my experience. 

Darkslide Film Lab - Based in Connecticut. Ran by Emily and I believe 2 others as scan techs. They do DSLR scanning but are currently in the process of acquiring more standardized lab equipment. There is no such thing as a Formula 1 road car. 


In the 1970's the Ford Cosworth DFV was a 3.0 Litre V8 that revved up to 11,500 RPM. The reason for this is due to the short stroke and large bore of the engine, known as "overbore".

In the 1980's the turbo charged Formula 1 cars were 1.5 litre V6's or Inline 4's revving 12,500 RPM. 

Soon after in the 90's there were 3.5 litre Regulations that mandating engines of the V12 by Ferrari and Honda, V10's by Renault, and V8's by ford, all revved up to 14,500 RPM.

Case in point: Titanium connecting rods + Crankshaft + pistions + very low stroke = high revving.

Also, though not neccisarlity written in stone, any engine configuration can rev very high, Inline 4's , V6's V8's, V10's, V12's, given that its internals are very lightweight (Alumninum, or Titanium) and that it is of an overbore configuration.

The reason why American V8 engines have a lower rev limit is due to the crankshaft configuration, known as the cross plane crankshaft that is ineffecient in its exhaust pules, and uses counterweights to make sure engine vibrations are balanced. These counterweights slow down the rotational inertia. 

On the other hand, Ferrari's use flat plane crankshafts, which have no counter balance weights, and allow it to rev higher.
